blocks.x: Cost per transaction, per customer, per inference — engineering metrics with P&L consequences.

The argument for FinOps is unit economics, not cost cutting is simple: decisions made on stale information cost more than the platform that would make them current — and the gap is measurable in weeks, not years.

items: Allocation architecture precedes optimization; unattributed spend is unmanageable spend.
Commitment strategy is a utilization game: 90%+ coverage without idle waste.
Architectural cost reviews redesign expensive paths before deployment, not after invoices.

blocks.x: Three questions to ask your current vendors

items: Ask for the baseline: how was the starting position measured, and who signed it?
Ask for the trail: can your auditors replay any decision the system made last week, end to end?
Ask for the unit cost: what does one decision cost to run, and who owns keeping it down?

blocks.x: Programs like FinOps is unit economics, not cost cutting rarely fail on the technology. They fail on unnamed ownership, unmeasured baselines and ungated scope — the three failure modes the guards on this page are built for.

items: Every stage has a gate with real stop authority — scope expands on measured deltas, not on momentum.
The operating model is designed first — who decides what, at which gate, holding which evidence.
Evidence is generated while the work happens, so the audit is a walkthrough, not an archaeology project.

blocks.x: Cloud unit costs typically fall 25-40% within two quarters of a disciplined FinOps program.
